stem: Which instrument is used to measure temperature?

options.rationale: A thermometer (or a digital temperature probe) measures temperature in °C.
A balance measures mass.
A stop-watch measures time.
A burette measures the volume of a liquid.

explanation: Temperature is measured with a thermometer, in degrees Celsius (°C).

stem: Match each quantity with the instrument used to measure it.
explanation: Time: stop-watch. Mass: balance. Volume of a gas: gas syringe. Temperature: thermometer. A burette measures the volume of a liquid.

stem: Which apparatus is most suitable for measuring the volume of hydrogen given off when magnesium reacts with dilute acid?

options.rationale: It collects the gas and measures its volume directly.

options.content: burette, used the normal way up
options.rationale: A burette measures liquids added from it, not gas given off.
A pipette measures one fixed volume of liquid.
A beaker cannot trap or measure a gas.

explanation: A gas syringe connected to the reaction flask collects the gas and shows its volume, usually to the nearest 1 cm³.

stem: On a thermometer, the marks labelled 20 °C and 30 °C have ten small divisions between them. The top of the liquid column is exactly on the 6th small mark above 20 °C. What is the temperature?
explanation: One division $= (30 - 20) \div 10 = 1$ °C. Six divisions above 20 °C is 26 °C.
hints: Work out what one small division is worth.

stem: True or false: a measuring cylinder measures 20 cm³ of acid more accurately than a burette.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: A burette has 0.1 cm³ divisions and is read to 0.05 cm³; a measuring cylinder is much less precise.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: a burette, read to 0.05 cm³, is more accurate than a measuring cylinder.

explanation: A burette has much finer divisions (0.1 cm³, read to 0.05 cm³) than a measuring cylinder (typically 0.5 cm³ to 1 cm³), so it measures volumes of liquid more accurately.

stem: A 250 cm³ measuring cylinder has numbered marks every 50 cm³, with ten small divisions between each pair of numbered marks. What volume does one small division represent?

options.rationale: Ten is the number of divisions, not the volume of each.
Each division must cover 50 ÷ 10 cm³.
50 cm³ is the gap between numbered marks.

explanation: The value of one division is the difference between numbered marks divided by the number of divisions: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 cm³.

stem: A thermometer has a small division for every 1 °C, with numbered marks every 10 °C. The top of the liquid column is halfway between the 4th and 5th small marks above 40 °C. Record the temperature.
explanation: Four divisions above 40 °C is 44 °C; halfway to the next mark adds 0.5 °C, giving 44.5 °C.
workedSolution:
1. One division $= 1$ °C.
2. $40 + 4 = 44$ °C, plus half a division: 44.5 °C.
hints: Estimate to the nearest half division.

stem: An electronic balance reads to 0.01 g. A sample has a mass of exactly four and a half grams. How should the mass be recorded?

options.rationale: Two decimal places, matching the balance.
This hides the fact that the balance shows hundredths of a gram.
The balance cannot show thousandths of a gram.
Rounding to the nearest gram throws away precision.

explanation: A measurement is recorded to the resolution of the instrument. This balance shows two decimal places, so the mass is written 4.50 g.

stem: Ammonia gas is produced in an experiment. Why should its volume be measured with a gas syringe rather than by collecting it over water?

options.content: A gas syringe can hold much larger volumes than a measuring cylinder.
options.rationale: Gas syringes usually hold only about 100 cm³.

options.content: Ammonia is very soluble, so much would dissolve in the water.
options.rationale: A gas syringe keeps the gas away from water.

options.content: Ammonia is denser than air, so it sinks out of the tube.
options.rationale: Ammonia is less dense than air, and density is not the problem.

options.content: Water turns ammonia into a different coloured gas.
options.rationale: Ammonia dissolves; it does not change colour.

explanation: Collection over water only works for gases that are not very soluble in water. Ammonia (like hydrogen chloride) dissolves readily, so a gas syringe is used.
hints: What happens when ammonia meets water?

stem: Complete the instruction for reading a measuring cylinder.

payload.template: Read the bottom of the {{blank:men}} with your eye at the same level, to avoid {{blank:par}} error.

explanation: The bottom of the meniscus is read with the eye level with it. Reading from above or below causes parallax error.

stem: Which pair of instruments is needed to measure the volume of carbon dioxide given off every 30 seconds when marble chips react with acid?

options.rationale: A thermometer measures temperature, not volume.
A ruler measures length; time is not measured.
Neither measures a gas volume or time.
One measures the volume, the other the time.

explanation: The volume of gas is read from a gas syringe at times measured with a stop-watch. (Another method follows the loss in mass on a balance, again with a stop-watch.)

stem: A student measures the temperature rise when dilute hydrochloric acid neutralises aqueous sodium hydroxide in a polystyrene cup.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: 25 cm³ of acid is needed, and a volume within about ±0.5 cm³ is acceptable. Which apparatus is the most sensible choice?

options.rationale: Beaker markings are too rough.
Gas syringes are for gases.
This measures only one fixed volume of 1 dm³.
Quick to use and precise enough for this experiment.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Why is a polystyrene cup used rather than a glass beaker?

options.content: Polystyrene reacts with the acid and adds heat.
options.rationale: Polystyrene is unreactive here.

options.content: Polystyrene is a good insulator, so less heat is lost.
options.rationale: Less heat loss gives a temperature rise closer to the true value.

options.content: Glass would dissolve slowly in the alkali.
options.rationale: Glass is not attacked at this concentration.

options.content: Polystyrene makes the reaction go faster.
options.rationale: The cup does not affect the rate.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The starting temperature is 21.5 °C and the highest temperature is 28.0 °C. Calculate the temperature rise.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest one advantage of using a digital thermometer that reads to 0.1 °C instead of a glass thermometer with 1 °C divisions.

points.description: Greater resolution/precision (reads to 0.1 °C), so smaller changes are measured more accurately; or no parallax/reading errors

parts.explanation: A digital thermometer reads to 0.1 °C, so the temperature change is measured more precisely, and there is no parallax error when reading it.

explanation: A measuring cylinder is precise enough here; the polystyrene cup reduces heat loss; the rise is 28.0 − 21.5 = 6.5 °C; a digital thermometer gives better resolution and avoids parallax.
hints: Match the precision of the apparatus to what the experiment needs.

stem: A student weighs by difference. A weighing bottle containing a solid has a mass of 18.36 g. After the solid is tipped into a beaker, the bottle has a mass of 15.84 g. Calculate the mass of solid transferred.
explanation: Mass transferred $= 18.36 - 15.84 = 2.52$ g.
hints: Subtract the final mass of the bottle from its starting mass.

stem: An electronic balance shows 0.02 g with nothing on the pan. Without zeroing it, a student weighs a sample and the balance shows 5.47 g. What is the true mass of the sample?

options.rationale: The zero error must be subtracted, not added.
Subtract the zero error: 5.47 − 0.02.
This ignores the zero error.
The zero error is 0.02 g, not 0.20 g.

explanation: The balance already reads 0.02 g too high (a zero error), so every reading is 0.02 g too large: 5.47 − 0.02 = 5.45 g. Pressing 'tare' before weighing avoids this.
hints: The balance adds 0.02 g to every reading.

stem: Choose the most suitable apparatus for each task.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Measuring about 50 cm³ of water to dissolve a solid before crystallisation.

options.rationale: Pipettes measure one fixed volume, e.g. 25.0 cm³, and are slow to use.
This is for gases.
Unnecessarily precise and slow for this task.
Approximate volumes are fine here.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Measuring exactly 10.0 cm³ of a solution that will be diluted accurately in a volumetric flask.

options.rationale: Not accurate enough for an accurate dilution.
Beaker markings are rough.
Conical flasks are not measuring instruments.
It delivers 10.0 cm³ very accurately.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Timing how long it takes for a cross under a flask to disappear.

options.rationale: This measures temperature.
This measures length.
It measures the time interval.
This measures mass.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why a measuring cylinder is acceptable in (a) but not in (b).

points.description: In (a) the exact volume of water does not affect the result (any reasonable volume dissolves the solid)
In (b) the volume decides the concentration of the diluted solution, so it must be measured accurately, which a measuring cylinder cannot do

parts.explanation: In (a) the volume of water only needs to be enough to dissolve the solid, so an error of a cm³ or two does not matter. In (b) the volume measured decides the concentration of the diluted solution, so it must be known accurately; a measuring cylinder is not accurate enough, so a volumetric pipette is used.

explanation: Match the apparatus to the accuracy needed: a measuring cylinder for rough volumes, a volumetric pipette for an accurately known volume, and a stop-watch for time.
hints: Does the exact volume affect the final result in each case?

stem: Which instrument has the smallest scale division for measuring a volume of liquid?

options.rationale: Its divisions are ten times larger.
Beaker markings are very rough.
It has the finest divisions.
Gas syringes measure gases, with 1 cm³ divisions.

explanation: A burette's divisions are 0.1 cm³ and it is read to 0.05 cm³, making it the most precise of these for liquids.

stem: True or false: a stop-watch that displays hundredths of a second allows a student to time a colour change by hand to the nearest 0.01 s.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: The display shows 0.01 s, but a person's reaction time is around 0.1–0.3 s, so hand timing is not that accurate.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: human reaction time (about 0.1–0.3 s) limits the accuracy, whatever the display shows.

explanation: The resolution of the display is 0.01 s, but starting and stopping by hand introduces errors of a few tenths of a second. Results are sensibly recorded to the nearest second (or 0.1 s at best).
hints: How quickly can a person press the button after seeing the change?

stem: Thandeka measures the temperature drop when ammonium nitrate dissolves in water. She uses a thermometer with 1 °C divisions, reading to the nearest 0.5 °C. The temperature falls from 22.0 °C to 19.0 °C.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Each reading could be wrong by up to 0.5 °C. Why does this make her result unreliable?

options.rationale: They can.

options.content: 0.5 °C is larger than the change she measured.
options.rationale: The change is 3 °C.

options.content: An error of about 1 °C is a large part of a 3 °C change.
options.rationale: Small changes are badly affected by reading errors.

options.content: The reading errors always cancel each other out.
options.rationale: They may add together.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest two improvements that would make the measured temperature change more reliable.

points.description: Use a thermometer with finer divisions (e.g. 0.1 °C or 0.2 °C) or a digital temperature probe
Use more ammonium nitrate (or less water) to give a larger temperature change
Insulate the container (polystyrene cup with lid) / stir and record the lowest temperature / repeat and take a mean

parts.explanation: Use a thermometer that reads to 0.1 °C (or a digital probe) so each reading is more precise; use more ammonium nitrate in the same volume of water so that the change is larger compared with the reading error; and insulate the container with a lid, stir well, record the lowest temperature and repeat to take a mean.

explanation: The change is 22.0 − 19.0 = 3.0 °C. With each reading uncertain by 0.5 °C, the change could be out by up to 1 °C, about a third of the result. A finer thermometer, a larger change and better insulation all improve reliability.
workedSolution:
1. (a) $22.0 - 19.0 = 3.0$ °C.
2. (b) Possible error $\approx 0.5 + 0.5 = 1$ °C, which is about 33% of 3.0 °C.
hints: Compare the size of the reading error with the size of the change.

stem: Which change would improve the accuracy of measuring out 20 cm³ of a solution with a measuring cylinder?

options.content: Use a 250 cm³ measuring cylinder instead of a 25 cm³ one.
options.rationale: Larger cylinders have coarser divisions.

options.content: Read the top of the meniscus.
options.rationale: The bottom of the meniscus should be read.

options.content: Use a 25 cm³ measuring cylinder instead of a 250 cm³ one.
options.rationale: A smaller cylinder has finer divisions, so the reading is more precise.

options.content: Look down on the scale from above.
options.rationale: This causes parallax error.

explanation: Measuring cylinders with a capacity just above the volume needed have the finest divisions, so they give the most accurate reading. Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
hints: Think about the size of the divisions.

stem: A strip of magnesium ribbon is laid along a ruler marked in millimetres. One end is at 2.0 cm and the other end is at 9.5 cm. What is the length of the ribbon in cm?
hints: The ribbon does not start at zero.
